question: A 13-year-old girl asks for an HIV self-test kit at OPD without a parent. Can she consent on her own?
change: Removed 'under the 2024 amendment'; added a patient so the answer must apply the current age of consent unprompted.
reference_answer: Yes. The age of consent for HIV self-testing is 12 years (2024 Amendment), reduced from 16 years in the 2022 guidelines, so a 13-year-old can consent herself.

She can consent on her own

question: Which clients skip the HIVST screen and go straight to routine HIV testing with the national algorithm?
change: Rephrased in clinician shorthand; content unchanged.
reference_answer: The priority groups get routine testing with the National HIV Testing Algorithm instead of the HIVST screen: malnourished and sick children, HIV-exposed children, clients with confirmed or presumptive TB, STI clients, index contacts, inpatients, pregnant and lactating women, and key populations. HIVST must also not be used for clients already known HIV-positive or on treatment.
must_include: Not for clients already HIV-positive or on ART
must_not_include: Pregnant women may use HIVST as their screen
Only a partial list presented as complete

question: 28-year-old man, reactive HIV self-test at OPD. Can I start ART on that result?
change: Shortened to clinician phrasing; content unchanged.
reference_answer: No. A single reactive HIV self-test is not a definitive diagnosis. He must be retested by a trained tester using the National HIV Testing Algorithm; confirmation cannot be done with another self-test. If confirmed positive, offer partner notification and link to treatment.
must_include: Do not start ART on a self-test result alone
Retest by a trained tester using the National HIV Testing Algorithm
Confirmation cannot be done with HIVST
must_not_include: ART can be started on the self-test result

question: A client wants to start injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA) PrEP. Can I use an HIV self-test to rule out HIV first?
change: Rephrased as a clinician's question; content unchanged.
reference_answer: No. For CAB-LA (and LEN), a rapid diagnostic test following the National HIV Testing Algorithm is needed before initiation and before every CAB-LA injection. An HIV self-test can be used to rule out HIV only before oral PrEP or the PrEP ring, and not for pregnant or breastfeeding women.
must_include: No, a self-test is not enough for CAB-LA
Use a rapid diagnostic test / National HIV Testing Algorithm before CAB-LA
must_not_include: An HIV self-test is acceptable before CAB-LA
check: verified in Amendment and PrEP 2025 (2025 adds LEN and testing before every CAB-LA injection)

question: Adult outpatient newly diagnosed with HIV, CD4 is 180. Should I send serum CrAg and urine TB-LAM?
change: Removed 'according to the 2024 amendment'; turned into a patient case so the current threshold must be applied.
reference_answer: Yes, both. Under the 2024 Amendment, CrAg screening and urine LF-LAM are done for PLHIV with CD4 ≤200 cells/mm³, for outpatients as well as inpatients. (In 2022 CrAg was at ≤100 and LF-LAM for outpatients at <100.) LF-LAM is also done regardless of CD4 if the patient has TB symptoms or is seriously ill.
must_include: Yes to both CrAg and urine LF-LAM
Applies to outpatients as well as inpatients
check: verified against the Amendment; NOTE the TB 2025 guideline (Table 52, p.205) lists CrAg at CD4 ≤100 'Yes' and ≤200 'may be considered' — clinician to confirm which threshold the benchmark expects

question: PLHIV diagnosed with TB on urine LF-LAM only, Xpert not confirmed. How do I classify it, and do the household contacts get TPT?
change: Turned into a case; kept as a natural two-part question (classification and its consequence).
reference_answer: Classify as bacteriologically confirmed TB (2024 Amendment; it was 'clinically diagnosed' in 2022), and by site as extrapulmonary TB when there is no Xpert confirmation. Because it is bacteriologically confirmed, the household contacts are eligible for TPT.
must_include: Extrapulmonary by site if no Xpert confirmation
Household contacts are eligible for TPT
must_not_include: Household contacts are not eligible for TPT

question: Adult on TLD for two years, viral load 450 copies/mL. How do I manage?
change: Shortened to clinician phrasing; content unchanged.
reference_answer: This is low-level viraemia (200-999 copies/mL under the 2024 Amendment). Give adherence counselling and assess adherence, tolerability and toxicity. Do not change the regimen unless there is toxicity or intolerance. Repeat the VL in 3 months. Genotyping is not recommended unless VL is ≥1000 copies/mL; consult the HIVDR clinical advisor if low-level viraemia persists.
must_include: Adherence counselling / assess adherence, tolerability, toxicity
No regimen change unless toxicity or intolerance
must_not_include: Switch to a second-line regimen now
Treat as suppressed and do nothing (2022 threshold <1000)

question: Breastfeeding woman on TLD, two undetectable viral loads since starting ART. How often should her routine VL be done now?
change: Was a four-group list question; now one patient, so the answer must pick the right group.
reference_answer: Every 6 months while she is breastfeeding. After the 3- and 9-month VLs and two consecutive undetectable results, routine VL is every 6 months for pregnant and breastfeeding women (also for children and adolescents 0-19 years and third-line clients); annual VL applies to other adults over 19.

question: Child living with HIV, 5 kg, starting first-line ART. Can I use the pALD (ABC/3TC/DTG 60/30/5 mg) dispersible tablet?
change: Was a two-part eligibility question; now one child at a weight band where pALD is not allowed.
reference_answer: No. pALD is for children weighing 6 kg up to 24.9 kg. A child of 3-5.9 kg must still use separate products: ABC/3TC 120/60 mg dispersible (1 tablet once daily at 3-5.9 kg) plus paediatric DTG. Separate products are also needed for children on rifampicin-based TB treatment and children on second/third line not previously on DTG.
must_include: No, pALD is not used below 6 kg
pALD weight range is 6 to 24.9 kg
Use separate ABC/3TC + paediatric DTG products
must_not_include: Any pALD tablet count for a 5 kg child

question: Breastfeeding mother of a 5-month-old has just tested HIV positive (new seroconversion). What do I do for the baby?
change: Turned into a case; reference expanded from the Amendment flowchart.
reference_answer: Test the infant immediately. If the infant is reactive, start ART as soon as possible. If negative, give the infant 3-drug PEP (2024 Amendment: 3-drug PEP after appropriate testing for breastfeeding infants of mothers found to have seroconverted), continuing until the mother is virally suppressed (undetectable). Start the mother on ART.
must_include: 3-drug PEP for the infant if negative
Continue until the mother is undetectable
must_not_include: Single-drug NVP prophylaxis as the full plan
Stop breastfeeding as a mandatory rule
check: verified; 'start the mother on ART' is general HIV care, not in these chunks — clinician to confirm wording

question: Client walks into my clinic after 8 months off ART; was on treatment at another facility and has no transfer letter. Do I register her as a new client?
change: Turned into a concrete case; content unchanged.
reference_answer: No. Do not decline services for lack of a transfer letter: continue re-engagement and contact the transferring facility to complete the transfer. A client verified as having interrupted treatment is not documented as new; re-link her to care under the re-engagement strategy, identify why she stopped and make an action plan. Do not do a pretreatment VL for clients returning to care. Having interrupted for 6 months or more, she should also be screened for advanced HIV disease.
must_include: Do not register as a new client
Do not refuse care without a transfer letter
Identify reasons for interruption / action plan
No pretreatment VL for re-engaging clients
must_not_include: Send her back for a transfer letter before treating

question: At a 30-week ANC visit the foetal heart rate is 104 beats/min. Is that normal?
change: Split a stitched two-part question (FHR + SFH); kept the FHR part as a case.
reference_answer: No. A normal foetal heart rate is 110-160 beats/minute; below 110 (or above 160) is abnormal, so 104 is abnormal and needs further assessment.
check: verified; the ANC guideline gives the range but no specific action for an abnormal FHR

question: Pregnant woman at her first ANC contact, RPR positive, no penicillin allergy. How do I treat?
change: Split a two-part question (testing interval + treatment); kept the treatment part as a case.
reference_answer: Give benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units IM stat, then weekly for 2 more doses (3 weekly doses in total). Encourage partner tracing and treatment, and take blood for TPHA at the next contact. If she were allergic to benzathine penicillin, refer to the STI guidelines for treatment; the newborn of a mother with a positive syphilis test also needs treatment after delivery.
must_not_include: A single dose of benzathine penicillin only
check: verified; ANC p.24 ('1 dose stat then weekly x2') and p.43 ('weekly for three weeks') agree on 3 doses

question: Pregnant woman, pre-pregnancy BMI 27. How much weight should she aim to gain?
change: Shortened; content unchanged.
reference_answer: 7-11.5 kg. A BMI of 27 is in the overweight range (25-29.9), for which the target gestational weight gain is 7-11.5 kg.

question: 24-year-old at her first ANC visit, healthy, Hb normal. Which daily supplements do I prescribe?
change: Turned into a case; content unchanged.
reference_answer: Daily oral iron and folic acid, 30-60 mg elemental iron plus 400 µg (0.4 mg) folic acid (the ANC tablet is 60 mg iron + 400 µg folic acid; give 3 months' supply and refill), and calcium 1.5 g daily. Routine multiple micronutrient supplements (multivitamins, vitamin D, E, B6, zinc, omega 3/6) are not recommended.
must_not_include: Folic acid 5 mg as the routine dose
Double-dose iron (that is for moderate anaemia)

question: Woman at 34 weeks with about 300 mL of vaginal bleeding, pulse normal, no signs of shock. How is this classified and what do I do at the clinic?
change: Was a definition question; now a case. Kept as a natural two-part question (classification and immediate action).
reference_answer: This is antepartum haemorrhage (bleeding from 28 weeks until delivery), classed as a major haemorrhage: 50-1000 mL without signs of shock. Shout for help; follow ABC; check vital signs and urgent Hb; insert 2 large IV lines and correct hypovolaemia with normal saline or Ringer's lactate; oxygen 4-6 L/min if available; group and cross-match; and refer to hospital as soon as possible. Do not perform a digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia is ruled out. Treat tachycardia seriously even if she looks stable.
must_include: Refer to hospital as soon as possible
No digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia is excluded

question: At the clinic, woman at 32 weeks, BP 165/112 with a persistent headache. What do I do before and during transfer?
change: Shortened; content unchanged.
reference_answer: This is severe pre-eclampsia (SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110 mmHg; persistent headache is a further severe feature). Refer to the regional referral hospital and, at the clinic/PHU, give a pre-referral loading dose of magnesium sulphate 4 g IM; she is then managed at hospital as per guidelines. If she convulses: do not leave her alone, shout for help, left lateral position, keep the airway clear, protect from injury, nothing in the mouth, oxygen 4-6 L/min by mask, and an IV line once the convulsion ends.
must_include: Urgent referral to the regional referral hospital
must_not_include: Mild pre-eclampsia / manage at the clinic
check: verified as printed (4 g IM). Earlier reviewer note: common regimens use a different IM loading dose; clinician to confirm

question: How many ANC contacts are recommended now, and at what gestational ages?
change: Kept general (schedule question); split from the ultrasound part.
reference_answer: At least 8 contacts (the WHO 2016 model, replacing the 4-visit focused ANC): the first in the first trimester (preferably 8-12 weeks), then at 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks.
must_include: First contact in the first trimester (8-12 weeks)
must_not_include: 4 visits (focused ANC) as the current model

question: Man diagnosed HIV positive two years ago, never started care, last seen 5 months ago. Is he eligible for Linkage Case Management?
change: Was a general eligibility list; now one client who meets one criterion.
reference_answer: Yes. LCM covers HIV-positive clients diagnosed in the facility or community who are newly diagnosed, who defaulted or disengaged and are returning as new patients, who were initiated in the community and referred to a facility, or who were previously diagnosed but have not received HIV care in the past 90 days. He meets the last criterion, and men are one of the groups given special attention.
must_include: Previously diagnosed with no HIV care in the past 90 days
must_not_include: Not eligible because he is not newly diagnosed

question: Client enrolled in LCM 6 months ago: on ART, adherent, disclosed to her sister, but only one contact has been tested. Can I discharge her from LCM?
change: Was a two-part question (duration + discharge criteria); now one client who fails one criterion.
reference_answer: Not yet. LCM runs to 180 days, and discharge requires all of: initiated and retained on ART to 6 months; disclosed to at least one person; adherent to the treatment plan; and at least two eligible contacts (partner, child or associate) tested for HIV, all documented in the CCF/CMIS. She has only one contact tested, so she does not yet meet the criteria.
must_include: At least two eligible contacts must be tested
Other criteria: retained on ART to 6 months, disclosed to at least one person, adherent
sources: unaids-linkages-sop-0043 (Linkages SOP p.30, discharge at day 180)

question: Adult with AKI, potassium 6.8 mmol/L. What emergency treatment and doses?
change: Removed 'do the NCD guidelines recommend'; content unchanged.
reference_answer: Hyperkalaemia ≥6 mmol/L: put the patient on a cardiac monitor. (1) Stabilise the myocardium with IV calcium gluconate 10%, 10 mL over 2 minutes (maximum 20 mL), not at the same time or in the same drip as sodium bicarbonate. (2) Shift potassium with ONLY 5 units of short-acting insulin (Actrapid) in 50 mL of 50% dextrose over 30 minutes (larger insulin doses accumulate in kidney failure and cause dangerous hypoglycaemia), and/or salbutamol nebuliser 10–20 mg every 1–2 hours, monitoring for tachycardia and arrhythmias. (3) A potassium binder such as sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) 15 g in 100 mL water once daily, unless there is bowel pathology. (4) If fluid-overloaded, IV furosemide 40–80 mg. (5) Urgent referral for dialysis (or acute peritoneal dialysis locally per protocol).
must_include: Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 2 min (max 20 mL)
Only 5 units Actrapid in 50 mL 50% dextrose over 30 min
must_not_include: Calcium gluconate in the same drip as sodium bicarbonate
Paediatric doses (0.5 mL/kg, 0.1 units/kg) for this adult

question: Adult with a severe asthma attack, talking in words, SpO2 90% on air. Immediate treatment and doses?
change: Removed 'do the NCD guidelines recommend'; added the severity features clinicians would give.
reference_answer: Oxygen to SpO2 94-98%. Salbutamol: nebulised 5 mg every 20 minutes for a severe attack (or 4-10 puffs by MDI + spacer every 20 minutes ×3 in the first hour). Add ipratropium bromide 0.5 mg to the nebuliser. Prednisolone 40-50 mg/day for 5-7 days. Because the attack is severe with SpO2 <92%, give IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes. Severe features mean admission/referral.
must_include: Salbutamol nebulised 5 mg every 20 min (or 4-10 puffs MDI + spacer every 20 min ×3)
IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min
must_not_include: Paediatric doses (2.5 mg salbutamol, 0.25 mg ipratropium, 25-75 mg/kg magnesium)

question: Outreach team tests a client HIV positive and starts ART in the community. By when must she be seen at a health facility?
change: Turned into a case; content unchanged.
reference_answer: Within 7 days. Clients testing HIV positive must be linked the same day or within 7 days of diagnosis, and seen at a health facility within 7 days whether or not they were initiated on ART; files from community initiation are transferred to the facility within 7 days. (Another section of the SOP says community-initiated clients must reach the facility 'within day 14'.)
must_include: Same day or within 7 days of diagnosis
Applies whether or not she was initiated in the community
must_not_include: No time limit once on ART
check: verified; the SOP is internally inconsistent (7 days on p.63-64, day 14 on p.61) — clinician to decide which the benchmark expects

question: What are the tracing steps for a client on ART who is more than 28 days late and can't be reached by phone?
change: Kept general (procedure question); shortened.
reference_answer: Verify the LTFU using the patient chart, CMIS/APMR and pharmacy records; contact the client by phone; if she cannot be reached after 3 phone attempts on different days (or times), refer to community expert clients for a home visit; if she still cannot be traced, use community partners for follow-up home visits.
must_include: 3 phone attempts on different days or times
Refer to community expert clients for home visit
Community partners if still not traced
must_not_include: Close the file as lost to follow-up without tracing
Home visit before any phone attempts

question: Palliative patient, pain well controlled on oral morphine 10 mg every 4 hours. I want to switch to twice-daily dosing. What dose, and what must I co-prescribe?
change: Was three-part; kept the conversion and co-prescription (natural pair), dropped the naloxone part.
reference_answer: Add up the 24-hour total: 10 mg × 6 = 60 mg in 24 hours, then divide by 2: 30 mg every 12 hours (the guideline calls this 'morphine PR', 30 mg twice daily). Always co-prescribe a laxative, e.g. a stimulant such as bisacodyl ('the hand that writes opioids should also write laxatives'); constipation is the most common side effect. Give an antiemetic if nausea occurs.
check: verified; 'morphine PR' as printed (likely prolonged release) — clinician to confirm the wording

question: Woman 4 months postpartum, exclusively breastfeeding on demand, periods not yet back. Can she rely on LAM for contraception?
change: Was 'list the three conditions'; now one woman who meets them.
reference_answer: Yes. LAM can be relied on when all 3 conditions are met: her menses have not returned since delivery, the baby is fully/exclusively breastfed on demand, and the baby is less than 6 months old. She meets all three; LAM is up to 98% effective under these conditions. She will need another method once any condition stops applying (e.g. at 6 months).
must_include: All 3 conditions: no menses, exclusive breastfeeding on demand, baby <6 months
must_not_include: LAM is not reliable at 4 months

question: Woman on progestin-only pills (Microval) missed 2 pills. What should she do?
change: Unchanged.
reference_answer: Take 2 pills as soon as possible and 2 more the next day, then return to her regular schedule on day 3, and use a backup method. (1 missed pill: take it as soon as possible, backup for 2 days; 3 missed pills: do not try to replace them, use backup and come to the facility.)
must_include: Back to the regular schedule on day 3

question: 38-year-old woman, smokes 10 cigarettes a day, wants a combined hormonal method. Which can't she use?
change: Rephrased in clinician wording; content unchanged.
reference_answer: Women aged 35 or older who smoke, regardless of how much, should not use combined oral contraceptives, the patch or the combined vaginal ring. The restriction on monthly combined injectables applies to women ≥35 who smoke 15 or more cigarettes a day, so at 10/day that rule does not exclude them. Progestin-only methods (pills, injectables, implants) are a good alternative; they can be used by smokers of any age.
must_include: Monthly injectable restriction is for ≥15 cigarettes/day
must_not_include: COCs are acceptable because she smokes fewer than 15 a day
Progestin-only methods are contraindicated in smokers

question: Exclusively breastfeeding mother, baby 2 months old, asks for the monthly injectable (Mesigyna). Can she start?
change: Shortened; content unchanged.
reference_answer: No, not yet. For an exclusively breastfeeding woman less than 6 months after birth, delay the first combined injectable until 6 months after giving birth or until breast milk is no longer the baby's main food, whichever comes first. Offer a progestin-only method instead.
must_include: Until 6 months after birth or breast milk no longer the main food, whichever comes first
must_not_include: She can start at 6 weeks postpartum

question: How long does a Jadelle implant last compared with Implanon NXT?
change: Kept general; removed 'described in the guidelines'.
reference_answer: Jadelle (2 levonorgestrel rods) is effective for 5 years; Implanon NXT/Nexplanon (1 etonogestrel rod) is labelled for up to 3 years. In heavier women, the effectiveness of levonorgestrel implants (Jadelle, Levoplant) may fall near the end of the labelled duration, so they may want earlier replacement.

question: Woman wants a copper IUCD; she delivered 4 days ago. When can it go in?
change: Shortened; content unchanged.
reference_answer: Not now. A postpartum IUCD can be inserted within 48 hours of birth (including caesarean delivery); after 48 hours, delay insertion until 4 weeks or more after birth. At day 4 she should come back from 4 weeks postpartum (if her menses have not returned, any time between 4 weeks and 6 months, reasonably certain she is not pregnant).
must_include: Within 48 hours of birth, otherwise wait
must_not_include: Wait until 6 weeks / 6 months as the rule

question: Woman had unprotected sex 4 days ago (about 96 hours). Is it too late for emergency contraception?
change: Was a list question (all EC options and windows); now one case that forces the right choice.
reference_answer: Too late for emergency contraceptive pills: the guideline gives ECPs within 72 hours of unprotected sex (the sooner, the more effective). A copper IUCD can still be inserted, as it can be used within 5 days of unprotected sex (prescribed and inserted by a doctor after pregnancy and STI are ruled out).
must_include: ECPs: within 72 hours, so outside the window
Copper IUCD within 5 days is still an option
must_not_include: Too late for any emergency contraception
check: verified; the guideline gives 72 hours for all ECPs including ulipristal (no 120-hour window stated)

question: Client took ulipristal (UPA) emergency contraception yesterday and wants to start combined pills. When can she start?
change: Turned into a case; content unchanged.
reference_answer: On the 6th day after taking UPA, because COCs and UPA interact (if both are present, one or both may be less effective). Give her the pills and tell her to start on day 6. She should use a backup method from when she took UPA until she has taken COCs for 7 days.
must_include: Start on the 6th day after UPA
Backup method until 7 days of COCs
must_not_include: Start COCs immediately (that applies to levonorgestrel/combined ECPs, not UPA)

question: A 15-year-old comes alone asking for an implant. Do I need a parent's consent?
change: Was 'do adolescents need consent and are any methods unsafe'; now one adolescent.
reference_answer: No. Contraceptive services should be available to adolescents without requiring authorization from a parent or guardian, and all contraceptives, including implants, are safe for adolescents and youth. The HIV guideline also notes that anyone aged 12 or older can give informed consent for family planning under the Child Welfare Act.
must_include: All contraceptives (including implants) are safe for adolescents
Age 12+ can consent to family planning
must_not_include: Parental or guardian consent is required
Implants are not suitable for adolescents
check: verified; the HIV 2022 key message on the same page says consent 'should be given by parents, guardians...' in the best interest of the child, which an answer could misapply

question: Woman on combined pills is starting rifampicin-based TB treatment. What do I tell her about her contraception?
change: Shortened; content unchanged.
reference_answer: Rifampicin (and rifabutin) may lower the effectiveness of COCs, so she needs a backup method (e.g. condoms) or a change of method. The same applies to progestin-only pills and monthly combined injectables. Emergency contraceptive pills can still be used by clients on rifampicin.
must_include: Use a backup method or change method

question: Woman living with HIV on an efavirenz-based regimen wants hormonal contraception. Which methods are least affected by her ART?
change: Unchanged.
reference_answer: DMPA: levels do not appear to be reduced by ARVs, including efavirenz. The levonorgestrel IUD is unlikely to be affected by ART. Efavirenz reduces progestin levels with COCs and may decrease the efficacy of levonorgestrel (Jadelle) and etonogestrel (Implanon) implants; levonorgestrel emergency pill levels are significantly reduced. Non-hormonal options (copper IUCD, condoms) are not affected.
must_include: Levonorgestrel IUD unlikely to be affected
Efavirenz may reduce implant efficacy (Jadelle, Implanon)
must_not_include: Implants are the best choice with efavirenz
Efavirenz does not affect any hormonal method
check: verified; the copper IUCD/condom sentence is general knowledge, not in Appendix 6 (which covers hormonal methods)

question: How often are CAB-LA and lenacapavir PrEP injections given?
change: Kept general; narrowed from all four PrEP products to the two injectables.
reference_answer: CAB-LA (cabotegravir 600 mg IM): two initiation injections one month apart, then every 2 months. LEN (lenacapavir 927 mg): two 1.5 mL subcutaneous injections every 26 weeks (6 months), plus an oral loading dose of 600 mg (2 × 300 mg tablets) on two consecutive days starting the day of the first injections. LEN needs the fewest visits.
must_include: CAB-LA: two injections 1 month apart, then every 2 months
LEN: two subcutaneous injections every 26 weeks / 6 months
LEN oral loading 600 mg on days 1 and 2

question: 27-year-old cisgender woman asks for event-driven (2+1+1) oral PrEP because she has sex only occasionally. Can she use it?
change: Was 'who can use ED-PrEP and how is it taken'; now a client it does not suit.
reference_answer: No. Event-driven PrEP is only for people assigned male at birth who are not using estradiol-based hormones; it is not recommended for people assigned female at birth. She should use daily oral PrEP: one tablet daily, starting 7 days before potential exposure and continuing for 7 days after the last potential exposure.
must_include: No, ED-PrEP is not recommended for her
ED-PrEP is only for people assigned male at birth not on estradiol
7 days before and 7 days after exposure

question: Woman starting daily oral PrEP. How many days before she is protected, and how long should she continue after her last exposure?
change: Kept as a natural two-part question (start and stop); minor rewording.
reference_answer: She needs 7 days of daily dosing before potential exposure, and should continue one tablet daily for 7 days after the last potential exposure before stopping.
must_include: 7 days of daily dosing before protection
Continue 7 days after the last exposure
must_not_include: Protected after a double dose 2-24 hours before sex
Stop 2 days after the last exposure (that rule is for people assigned male at birth)

question: 16-year-old weighing 33 kg wants CAB-LA PrEP. Is she eligible?
change: Was a table question (age and weight limits for every product); now one client near a cut-off.
reference_answer: Not for CAB-LA. She meets the age criterion (≥16 years) but CAB-LA requires a body weight of at least 35 kg (also for LEN). At 33 kg she can use oral PrEP or the PrEP ring, which require ≥30 kg.
must_include: Oral PrEP or ring (≥30 kg) are options

question: Client wants to start PrEP; condomless sex with a partner of unknown status 36 hours ago. What do I do?
change: Shortened; content unchanged.
reference_answer: Assess for PEP instead of PrEP, because the exposure was within the past 72 hours. If eligible, start PEP. Retest for HIV at the end of the 28-day PEP course; if HIV negative and otherwise eligible, she can move straight to PrEP without a gap.
must_include: PEP assessment, not PrEP, because exposure <72 hours
Transition to PrEP after 28 days of PEP if HIV negative, without a gap

question: Client wanting PrEP has fever, sore throat and rash; condomless sex 10 days ago; HIV test today negative. Do I start PrEP?
change: Shortened; content unchanged.
reference_answer: No. Symptoms of acute HIV infection with a possible exposure in the previous 14 days mean suspected AHI: defer PrEP for 4 weeks, give exposure-reduction counselling and STI screening, and repeat the HIV test after 4 weeks; if still negative and otherwise eligible, start PrEP. (PEP does not apply: the exposure was more than 72 hours ago.)
must_include: Do not start PrEP now / defer
must_not_include: Start PrEP today because the test is negative

question: Woman on rifampicin-based TB treatment wants injectable PrEP. Can she start CAB-LA or lenacapavir?
change: Unchanged.
reference_answer: Not while on rifampicin. Rifampicin (and rifapentine, rifabutin for LEN) significantly reduces cabotegravir and lenacapavir levels, so they should not be co-administered. CAB-LA can be considered 2 weeks after she completes rifampicin/rifapentine; she should not initiate LEN while on TB treatment. (A client already on LEN who starts rifampicin can continue with supplemental LEN doses.) Oral PrEP or the PrEP ring are options meanwhile.
must_include: CAB-LA can be considered 2 weeks after rifampicin is completed
Oral PrEP or ring as alternatives
must_not_include: Start CAB-LA with a dose adjustment
Start LEN with supplemental doses (that applies only to clients already on LEN)

question: Client on lenacapavir PrEP comes back 30 weeks after her last injection, no oral bridging. What do I do?
change: Shortened; content unchanged.
reference_answer: Re-test for HIV and clinically reassess (PEP indication, suspected acute HIV infection). Because more than 28 weeks have passed without bridging, restart the initiation regimen: day 1, two subcutaneous injections plus 2 oral LEN tablets (300 mg each); day 2, two more tablets; then schedule the next injection in 26 weeks. (Within 28 weeks she would simply have received the follow-up injection.)
must_include: More than 28 weeks: restart the initiation regimen
must_not_include: Just give the routine follow-up injection

question: Woman using a contraceptive vaginal ring wants the dapivirine PrEP ring as well. Can she have it?
change: Was 'how effective is the ring and who should not use it'; now one client with a contraindication.
reference_answer: No. Women using contraceptive vaginal rings or a diaphragm should not be given the PrEP ring. Offer another PrEP method (oral PrEP, CAB-LA or LEN, if eligible). Other contraindications: people assigned male at birth, exposure through anal sex or needle sharing, and allergy to dapivirine.
must_include: Contraceptive vaginal ring (or diaphragm) is a contraindication

question: 52-year-old on oral PrEP, estimated creatinine clearance 55 mL/min (confirmed). What do I do?
change: Added 'confirmed' to match the guideline's stopping rule.
reference_answer: Stop oral PrEP: it is stopped when a creatinine elevation is confirmed and the estimated CrCl falls below 60 mL/min. Look for other causes with the medical officer, recheck creatinine for another 1-3 months, and restart oral PrEP if CrCl returns above 60 mL/min. Other methods (PrEP ring, CAB-LA, LEN) do not carry this kidney restriction and can be offered.

Send an HIV genotype (required for seroconverters and anyone exposed to CAB-LA in the last 12 months), but do not delay ART for the result. reference_answer: Yes. A positive HBsAg is not a contraindication to PrEP. Take LFTs and platelets to rule out active hepatitis (calculate the APRI score if possible), monitor LFTs every 6 months and when she stops oral PrEP, and refer to a medical officer if she wants to stop oral PrEP, because of the risk of hepatitis B viral rebound. question: 28-year-old man: low mood and loss of interest for 3 weeks, poor sleep, poor appetite, tiredness and poor concentration. Does he meet criteria for major depressive disorder?
change: Was 'list the diagnostic criteria in the Mental Health Desk Guide'; removed the document name and turned into a case.
reference_answer: Yes. MDD requires symptoms for at least 2 weeks, with depressed mood and/or markedly diminished interest or pleasure most of the day nearly every day, plus 4-5 other symptoms (e.g. disturbed sleep, disturbed appetite or weight change, poor concentration, psychomotor change, guilt, worthlessness/hopelessness, fatigue, body pains, recurrent thoughts of death or suicide). He has both core symptoms for 3 weeks plus 4 others (sleep, appetite, fatigue, concentration). Screen for suicide risk.

question: 45-year-old woman with moderate depression and recent suicidal thoughts, starting medication. Amitriptyline or an SSRI, and at what starting dose?
change: Was three-part (all first-line doses + when to prefer amitriptyline); now one patient where the choice matters.
reference_answer: An SSRI. Fluoxetine and sertraline are preferred when there is suicidality (and when sedation is not wanted, in the elderly, children and frail patients); tricyclics can be fatal in overdose and should be avoided as far as possible in patients with suicidal thoughts. Start fluoxetine 10-20 mg once daily (max 60-80 mg/day) or sertraline 25-50 mg at bedtime (max 200 mg/day). Do a suicide risk assessment at every visit; SSRIs can cause agitation and increased suicide risk in the first 2-4 weeks.

Fluoxetine 10-20 mg daily or sertraline 25-50 mg at bedtime

question: 10-year-old boy with depression. Can I start an antidepressant?

reference_answer: No. Under 12 years, do not prescribe antidepressants: provide counselling and refer (children with MDD are managed at the specialised psychiatric hospital level).

question: Patient scores 22 on the Suicide Risk Assessment Form. What is the risk level and what do I do?
change: Shortened; content unchanged.
reference_answer: High risk (21-30): immediate assessment by a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist; psychiatric admission is recommended and involuntary admission may be required. Do not leave the person alone and remove means of self-harm. (0-10 low: may go home with advice; 11-20 medium: assessment by a health professional, consider admission.)

question: Adult scores 16 on the PHQ-9. What does that mean and how should it be treated?
change: Was 'how are PHQ-9 scores interpreted' (whole table); now one score.
reference_answer: A score of 15-19 is major depression of moderate severity (called 'moderately severe' in the HIV Amendment and PrEP charts). question: Patient on an efavirenz-based ART regimen needs a mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder. Can I use carbamazepine?
change: Was a general question; now one patient.
reference_answer: Avoid it. Carbamazepine, phenytoin and phenobarbital should be avoided in patients on ART because they interact with NNRTIs and protease inhibitors (the Mental Health Desk Guide says they reduce their levels). Use sodium valproate (preferred in PLHIV) or lamotrigine instead; patients already on these anticonvulsants should be switched to lamotrigine, levetiracetam or sodium valproate CR.

question: Patient with bipolar disorder presents in a depressive episode. Can I start fluoxetine on its own?
change: Turned into a case; content unchanged.
reference_answer: No. An antidepressant alone may precipitate a manic episode in bipolar disorder. For the depressive phase, give a mood stabiliser plus an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic (the HIV 2022 guideline: mood stabiliser plus antidepressant, adding an antipsychotic if there are psychotic features). If mania emerges, stop the antidepressant immediately and refer.

question: Adult with mild alcohol withdrawal (tremor, sweating, no confusion or seizures). What do I prescribe?
change: Was two-part (withdrawal + Wernicke thiamine); kept the withdrawal regimen as a case.
reference_answer: Chlordiazepoxide 10-20 mg 8-hourly for 2-5 days (maximum 250 mg/24 hours), then taper the total daily dose by 25-50% per day over 2-5 days down to 5 mg daily. Add thiamine according to risk: 100 mg orally daily for a month for mild thiamine deficiency; high-risk patients get 200-500 mg IV/IM 12-hourly for 3-5 days, then 250-300 mg/day orally for a month.
must_include: Taper by 25-50% per day to 5 mg

question: Acute psychosis, severely agitated, needs rapid tranquillisation. Which medicines, doses and daily maximums?
change: Removed 'does the Mental Health Desk Guide list'.
reference_answer: Haloperidol IM 5 mg stat, repeated every half hour if still agitated (maximum 18-20 mg/day), OR chlorpromazine IM 100-150 mg stat, repeated every 4-6 hours if still agitated (maximum 600-800 mg/day). Either may be followed by diazepam IV 10-20 mg stat (maximum 20 mg/day) OR lorazepam IV 2-4 mg stat (maximum 4 mg/day). Avoid chlorpromazine in the elderly, adolescents and epilepsy.

question: What's the syndromic treatment for male urethral discharge?
change: Kept general (standard regimen question); reference corrected to include metronidazole from Chart 3.
reference_answer: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM stat (or cefixime 400 mg orally stat) plus azithromycin 1 g orally stat, to cover gonorrhoea and chlamydia; the syndromic chart (Chart 3) and the summary table also add metronidazole 2 g orally stat for trichomonas. Give the health promotion package (condoms, partner notification slips, HIV testing), and follow up after 7 days. Second-line options: spectinomycin 2 g IM or gentamicin 240 mg IM for gonorrhoea; doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days for chlamydia.

question: Pregnant woman with a genital ulcer who is allergic to penicillin. How do I treat?
change: Was two-part (standard GUS regimen + pregnant/allergic); kept the higher-risk case.
reference_answer: Replace benzathine penicillin with erythromycin (base/stearate) 500 mg orally QID for 14 days. The rest of the genital ulcer regimen covers chancroid and herpes (the standard regimen is benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM stat + azithromycin 1 g stat + acyclovir 400 mg TDS for 7 days). Because erythromycin does not adequately treat the foetus, the newborn must be treated soon after delivery.

question: Non-pregnant woman with vaginal discharge; STI risk assessment is negative. How do I treat?
change: Was a comparison of two groups; now the risk-negative case only.
reference_answer: A negative risk assessment points to vaginitis, so treat bacterial vaginosis and candidiasis: metronidazole 2 g orally stat plus clotrimazole 500 mg pessary intravaginally at night. Advise her to avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for 24-48 hours after the last dose. (A positive risk assessment would add ceftriaxone 1 g IM + azithromycin 1 g to cover cervical infection.)

question: Woman 10 weeks pregnant with lower abdominal pain and cervical motion tenderness, suspected PID. Can I treat her as an outpatient?
change: Was 'when should she be hospitalised'; now one case that meets a criterion.
reference_answer: No. Suspected PID in a pregnant woman should be referred for hospitalisation and further management, because of the high risk of maternal morbidity, fetal wastage and preterm delivery. Hospitalisation should also be considered when the diagnosis is uncertain, surgical emergencies (appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy) cannot be excluded, or a pelvic abscess is suspected. Any PID patient who has not responded within 3 days, or worsens, must be referred.

question: Patient treated for syphilis 6 months ago still has a positive TPHA. Is that treatment failure, and which test should I use to monitor her?
change: Was a test-comparison question; now a case where confusing the tests causes harm. Kept as a natural two-part question.
reference_answer: No, not by itself. Treponemal tests (TPHA, RDT/Tp, TPPA, FTA) stay positive for life after successful treatment, so they cannot be used to monitor treatment. Monitor with a non-treponemal test (RPR/VDRL), which can be quantified: record the baseline titre and repeat at 3, 6 and 12 months; a fourfold decline in titre means adequate response.

Treponemal tests remain positive for life

question: Well baby at birth; mother had a reactive syphilis test in pregnancy and was treated. What do I do for the baby?
change: Added the detail that the mother was treated (the rule applies either way).
reference_answer: Give the baby a single IM dose of benzathine penicillin 50,000 IU/kg, whether or not the mother was treated. Examine at birth and every 3 months until serology is confirmed to be, and remain, negative. Hospitalise babies who are symptomatic. (Confirmed early congenital syphilis is treated with aqueous penicillin 50,000 IU/kg IV 12-hourly for the first 7 days of life and 8-hourly thereafter, 10 days in total, or procaine penicillin 50,000 IU/kg IM daily for 10 days.)

Even though the mother was treated
Follow-up every 3 months until serology negative

question: Baby 5 days old with purulent discharge from both eyes. How do I treat the baby and the breastfeeding mother?
change: Turned into a case; kept as a natural two-part question (baby and mother).
reference_answer: Neonatal conjunctivitis is a medical emergency: treat within 24 hours to prevent blindness. Treat the baby for both gonorrhoea and chlamydia: ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM single dose (maximum 125 mg) plus erythromycin syrup 50 mg/kg/day orally in 4 divided doses for 14 days, and clean the eyes with saline or distilled water. Mother: ceftriaxone 1 g IM stat (or cefixime 400 mg orally stat) plus azithromycin 1 g orally stat (or erythromycin 500 mg QID for 7 days). Examine and treat the partner too.

question: Man with chronic hepatitis B: HBV DNA 5,000 IU/mL, ALT 45 U/L, no cirrhosis, HIV negative. Does he need antiviral treatment?
change: Removed 'under the updated (2024 WHO-aligned) criteria'; now one patient.
reference_answer: Yes. Under the 2024 criteria, treatment is recommended when HBV DNA is >2000 IU/mL together with ALT above the upper limit of normal (30 U/L for men, 19 U/L for women); he has both. (Other criteria: significant fibrosis or cirrhosis by APRI/elastography; special risk factors such as HIV/HDV/HCV coinfection, family history of liver cancer, immunosuppression, diabetes; or, without HBV DNA testing, persistently abnormal ALT.) First-line treatment is tenofovir (TDF) or entecavir monotherapy.

question: Pregnant woman, HBsAg positive, HIV negative; HBV DNA testing not available. What do I do to prevent transmission to the baby?
change: Added HIV-negative so the answer cannot default to ART.
reference_answer: Offer tenofovir (TDF) prophylaxis (where DNA/HBeAg testing is unavailable, offer to all HBsAg-positive pregnant women), ideally from at least the second trimester until delivery. Give the infant hepatitis B birth-dose vaccine within 24 hours, then the EPI schedule. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated and caesarean section is not indicated for HBV. Test the infant for HBsAg at 6–12 months.

From at least the second trimester until delivery
Birth-dose hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours

Caesarean section to prevent HBV transmission

question: 40-year-old woman with a reactive anti-HCV rapid test. Does she have hepatitis C, and how will I know she's cured after treatment?
change: Turned into a case; kept as a natural two-part question.
reference_answer: Not yet confirmed. A reactive antibody test shows exposure only; confirm current infection with HCV RNA (or HCV core antigen). If viraemic, treat with a pangenotypic DAA regimen (no genotyping needed; usually 12 weeks). Cure is an undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after completing treatment (SVR12).

Cure = undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after treatment (SVR12)

question: 28-year-old woman presents 20 hours after a sexual assault. What presumptive STI treatment do I give, and what else must be done today?

reference_answer: Presumptive STI treatment: ceftriaxone (or cefixime 400 mg, or spectinomycin 2 g IM) plus azithromycin 1 g stat (or doxycycline 100 mg 12-hourly for 7 days) plus metronidazole 2 g stat (or 400 mg 12-hourly for 7 days). question: Adult at OPD with a cough for 4 days, no fever, night sweats or weight loss. Is he presumptive TB?
change: Was a definition question; now one patient with a single symptom.
reference_answer: Yes. Any one of the four TB symptoms (cough of any duration, fever, night sweats, unintended weight loss) defines presumptive TB, so a cough of 4 days counts. Investigate with Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra. (Other screening criteria: a positive CAD/AI chest X-ray reading, or CRP >5 mg/L in ART-naive PLHIV over 10 years; in children under 10, TB contact alone.)

Not presumptive without fever or weight loss

question: PLHIV with CD4 of 150 and no TB symptoms. Which TB tests should I do?

reference_answer: Do a urine LF-LAM: it is indicated for PLHIV with advanced HIV disease (CD4 <200 or WHO stage 3/4) regardless of TB symptoms. If LF-LAM is positive, start TB treatment and also send Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra; if negative, apply the advanced HIV disease package and give TPT if eligible. (Xpert Ultra is the initial test for anyone with presumptive TB.)

Xpert Ultra if LAM positive / presumptive TB

question: HIV-negative adult with no previous TB has an Xpert Ultra result 'MTB trace detected' on sputum. What do I do?
change: Shortened; reference rewritten because the guideline's text and algorithm disagree for this group.
reference_answer: The guideline is internally inconsistent here. Its text (4.3.1) says that in HIV-negative persons an initial trace result should be repeated on a fresh specimen and the second Ultra result used for decisions (a second trace is enough to diagnose pulmonary TB unless there is recent previous TB). Its Figure 17 algorithm puts HIV-negative patients with no previous TB in the 'treat' branch, and limits repeat testing to those with previous TB. In all cases send culture and DST (Xpert XDR, pDST) to check rifampicin resistance.

question: New adult TB patient, 60 kg, drug-susceptible pulmonary TB. Regimen and number of tablets?
change: Added 'drug-susceptible pulmonary' so the 6-month regimen clearly applies.
reference_answer: 2RHZE/4RH. At 55-70 kg: 4 tablets daily of RHZE 150/75/400/275 mg for the 2-month intensive phase, then 4 tablets daily of RH 150/75 mg for the 4-month continuation phase. Give pyridoxine with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy.

question: In drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, when are follow-up sputum smears done, and can Xpert be used to monitor response?
change: Kept general; natural two-part question.
reference_answer: Send a sputum smear (2 samples, 'spot, spot' or 'spot, early morning') at the end of month 2, and again at the end of month 5 and the end of treatment (month 6). Do not use Xpert MTB/RIF to monitor treatment response; routine chest X-ray monitoring is also not recommended.
must_include: End of month 2, month 5 and month 6
Xpert should NOT be used to monitor treatment

question: Adult on drug-susceptible TB treatment is still smear positive at month 5. What is the treatment outcome and what do I do?
change: Was a definition question (failure and LTFU); now one patient who meets the failure definition.
reference_answer: Treatment failure: sputum smear positive at 5 months or later (or culture positive at 2 months). Assess adherence and clinical condition, check baseline DST to rule out drug resistance, repeat Xpert Ultra and/or Xpert MTB/XDR, and send a sample for sequencing, culture and phenotypic DST; manage as DR-TB if resistance is found. (A previously treated 'failure' case is re-registered and referred for DR-TB treatment.)
must_include: Smear positive at month 5 or later
Check for drug resistance (Xpert XDR, culture/DST, sequencing)

question: 5-year-old with pulmonary TB confined to one lobe, no cavities, Xpert 'trace', mild symptoms, not needing admission, no TB treatment before. Which regimen?
change: Was 'which children can receive the 4-month regimen'; now one child meeting the criteria.
reference_answer: The 4-month regimen: 2HRZ(E)/2HR. Children aged 3 months to under 16 years with non-severe TB (disease confined to one lobe without cavities or miliary pattern, Xpert negative/trace/very low/low, mild symptoms not needing hospitalisation) and no TB treatment in the past 2 years get 2 months of HRZ(E) then 2 months of HR. Severe TB or severe malnutrition gets 6 months (2HRZE/4HR).

question: Newly diagnosed HIV, started treatment for pulmonary TB 5 days ago. When do I start ART, and which regimen?
change: Was two-part (timing + TB meningitis difference); dropped the meningitis part and asked for the regimen instead.
reference_answer: Start ART as soon as possible, preferably within 2 weeks of starting TB treatment (same day if clinically stable), regardless of CD4. Use TDF 300 mg/3TC 300 mg once daily plus DTG 50 mg twice daily (because of rifampicin), returning to DTG 50 mg once daily two weeks after TB treatment is completed.

Back to once daily 2 weeks after TB treatment ends
must_not_include: DTG 50 mg once daily with rifampicin
Wait until TB treatment is finished

question: Patient started TB treatment, then ART 3 weeks ago; now fever and worsening lymph nodes. What is this likely to be, and how do I manage it?
change: Added typical features; content unchanged.
reference_answer: Likely paradoxical TB-associated IRIS. First exclude other infections (and drug resistance or poor adherence). Continue anti-TB treatment and ART; most cases respond to symptomatic therapy: NSAIDs or corticosteroids, prednisone 20-70 mg/day for 5-12 weeks, or IV methylprednisolone 40 mg every 12 hours if severe. ART interruption is rarely needed, except in life-threatening (especially neurological) presentations.

question: 26-year-old woman, 20 weeks pregnant, newly diagnosed rifampicin-resistant pulmonary TB. Can she have BPaLM?

reference_answer: No. BPaLM (6 months of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin) is the preferred regimen for MDR/RR-TB, but pregnant and lactating women are not eligible. The alternative for her is the 6-month Bdq-Dlm-Lfx-Lzd-Cfz regimen, for which pregnant and lactating women are eligible (adjusted once FQ DST is available: FQ-susceptible, omit Cfz; FQ-resistant, omit Lfx).

question: Baby born to a mother who started TB treatment 3 weeks before delivery. What do I do for the baby?

reference_answer: High risk (delivered within 8 weeks of maternal treatment start): screen the newborn immediately and investigate the placenta for congenital TB. Treat if symptomatic; otherwise give TPT for 3 or 6 months and withhold BCG until 2 weeks after TPT is completed (repeat BCG if it was given just before TPT). Breastfeeding continues with IPC measures (mask, ventilation). If the mother has MDR-TB, consult an expert.

question: HIV-negative adult living with a patient who has MDR-TB. Which TB preventive treatment do I give?

Isoniazid- or rifamycin-based regimens (6H, 3HP, 3HR) do not cover MDR-TB.

question: Nurse had a needlestick from an HIV-positive patient 3 hours ago. Which PEP regimen, and for how long?

reference_answer: Start three-drug PEP now: tenofovir (TDF) + lamivudine (3TC) + dolutegravir (DTG) for 28 days. If DTG is unavailable or contraindicated, ATV/r, DRV/r, LPV/r or RAL can be the third drug. question: Health worker was splashed with urine (not blood-stained) from an HIV-positive patient. Does she need PEP?

reference_answer: No. Exposure to body fluids that do not pose a significant risk (tears, non-blood-stained saliva, urine and sweat) does not require PEP. PEP is also not needed when the exposed person is already HIV positive, or when the source is confirmed HIV negative (unless the source may be in the window period).

question: Woman arrives 10 hours after a sexual assault without a police form. Can I start PEP, and what else should I offer?

reference_answer: Yes. PEP is started at first contact even without the police form (RSP88). question: 9-month-old HIV-exposed infant, still breastfeeding. Which test do I use to check HIV status?

question: How often should HIV-negative pregnant women who are not on PrEP be retested for HIV?
change: Kept general (schedule question); content unchanged.
reference_answer: Every 2 months, aligned with her scheduled ANC visits, with the most important retest in the third trimester at 34 weeks. Keep offering PrEP at each visit (opt-out). After delivery, retest while breastfeeding at 6 weeks, 14 weeks, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18 months, aligned with the mother-baby pair schedule.

question: What is the viral load schedule for a pregnant woman already on ART, through breastfeeding?

reference_answer: VL at the first ANC visit (regardless of when the last one was done), again at 34 weeks, a compulsory VL at 6 weeks after delivery, then every 6 months until breastfeeding stops. (Women newly starting ART get their first VL 3 months after initiation.)

question: When is an HIV-exposed newborn first tested for HIV, and with which test?
